title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Odbcconf
summary: Odbcconf.exe is a Microsoft-signed Windows utility whose stated purpose is to configure Open Database Connectivity drivers and data source names, and it is normally driven by a response file that lists the configuration actions to perform. Among its supported actions is a REGSVR directive that registers a library file with the operating system, which means the tool can be pointed at an arbitrary dynamic-link library and will cause that library's registration entry point to execute. An adversary uses this in the same spirit as the Regsvr32 technique that is often called squiblydoo, but through a different trusted binary, in the hope that application control and monitoring rules cover the better-known carrier and overlook this one. The activity is notable for how little it resembles its own legitimate purpose: the command is issued with silent and action switches that reference a file in a temporary, download or public folder, and no database driver or data source configuration actually changes as a result. Detection therefore combines process creation telemetry for odbcconf.exe with those arguments, child processes that a database configuration tool would never need, and the absence of corresponding ODBC registry or configuration changes. Genuine use is rare, scripted, references vendor driver packages under trusted paths, and produces the configuration outcome it was invoked for.

beginner.definition: ODBC stands for Open Database Connectivity, a standard way for programs to talk to databases. Odbcconf.exe is a small Windows tool that sets up database drivers and connection entries. It is signed by Microsoft, so security tools usually trust it.
beginner.whyItMatters: The tool also has an action that registers a library file with Windows. An attacker can use that action to register their own library file, and Windows runs its start-up code. Nothing about the database setup actually changes, so the tool looks busy but produces no normal result. If you ignore this, a rare program can become a quiet way to run code.
howItWorks: ODBC is a standard way for programs to talk to databases, and its full name is Open Database Connectivity.
Each database connection needs a driver and a small configuration entry, called a data source name.
Administrators use odbcconf.exe to create these entries, usually with a silent switch and an answer file.
The tool also supports an action named REGSVR, which registers a library file with Windows.
An attacker uses that action to register a library file they wrote, so Windows executes its start-up code.
The connection settings are never really changed, so nothing in the database world looks different afterwards.
beginner.example: In a large bank, a technician in overalls can walk to the machines because everyone assumes a technician belongs there. This technician carries no tools for the machines, only a small box that they plug in and leave running. The staff looked at the overalls and never asked to see the work order. odbcconf.exe is the overalls, and the library file is the box.
takeaways: odbcconf.exe can register a library file even when no database work is happening.
Its use is rare on workstations, so any appearance is worth reviewing.
Read the file path inside the command, not only the name of the tool.

objectives: Explain what ODBC is and what odbcconf.exe is designed to configure.
Describe how the REGSVR action can be repurposed to run a library file.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the System Binary Proxy Execution parent technique.
Explain how this abuse resembles and differs from scriptlet abuse through Regsvr32.
Identify the command line and supporting evidence that shows odbcconf abuse rather than real database configuration.
